item.content:encoded:
The Council of Europe Youth Department, together with the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe and in partnership with DemNet Foundation, has opened applications for an international capacity-building workshop on Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies.

Titled “Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies: How to Start?”, the workshop will take place from 19 to 21 October 2026 at the European Youth Centre Budapest, Hungary.

This opportunity is designed for young activists, civil society representatives, local and regional government representatives, youth-centre staff, political education practitioners and other people who are interested in democratic participation and have a concrete interest in establishing citizens’ assemblies or other deliberative processes.

The workshop will provide practical training on how citizens’ assemblies work, how they can be planned and implemented, and how organisations and local or regional authorities can develop the institutional and political support needed to make such processes successful.

Selected participants will have their travel, accommodation and meals covered for the duration of the workshop, in accordance with Council of Europe rules.

The application deadline is 7 September 2026.

Opportunity Overview

  • Opportunity: Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies: How to Start?
  • Organisers: Council of Europe Youth Department and Congress of Local and Regional Authorities
  • Partner: DemNet Foundation
  • Opportunity type: International capacity-building workshop
  • Location: European Youth Centre Budapest, Hungary
  • Workshop dates: 19–21 October 2026
  • Expected arrival: 18 October 2026
  • Departure: 21 October 2026
  • Application deadline: 7 September 2026
  • Participants: Approximately 30
  • Minimum age: 18
  • Nationality requirement: Citizen of a Council of Europe member state
  • Working language: English
  • English requirement: Working-level English
  • Travel: Covered for selected participants
  • Accommodation: Covered for selected participants
  • Meals: Covered for selected participants
  • Application: Online application form

The official call confirms that applications submitted after 7 September 2026 cannot be considered.

What Is the Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies Workshop?

Citizens’ assemblies are a form of deliberative democracy in which ordinary citizens are brought together to learn about an issue, consider different perspectives, deliberate collectively and develop recommendations.

They can provide communities with structured ways of involving citizens in important public decisions.

The Council of Europe workshop is designed to move beyond simply explaining the concept of citizens’ assemblies. It is a hands-on capacity-building experience intended to help participants understand what is required to actually design and implement one.

According to the official call, participants should leave the workshop with a strong understanding of:

  • How citizens’ assemblies work
  • How to plan and organise an assembly
  • How to develop an appropriate question or topic
  • How to establish effective governance arrangements
  • How to recruit participants
  • How to facilitate the deliberative process
  • How information and recommendations are handled
  • How to connect the process with public administration
  • How to build political and institutional support
  • How citizens’ assemblies can operate at local and regional levels

The workshop will particularly focus on helping participants take these ideas back to their own organisations, municipalities, regions or communities.

Why Is This Workshop Being Organised?

The workshop forms part of the Council of Europe programme “Strengthening Democratic Resilience through Youth Engagement and Deliberative Democracy.”

The programme was launched in September 2025 and is scheduled to continue through May 2027.

Its broader objective is to strengthen awareness and practical capacity for deliberative democracy, with a particular emphasis on youth citizens’ assemblies, across Council of Europe member states.

The initiative builds on several important European democratic participation frameworks, including the Committee of Ministers’ recommendation on deliberative democracy, the Congress’s recommendations concerning deliberative methods in European municipalities and regions, and the European Charter on the Participation of Young People in Local and Regional Life.

The workshop therefore sits within a wider effort to strengthen democratic participation and create more meaningful opportunities for young people and citizens to contribute to public decision-making.

What Will Participants Learn?

The workshop is structured around practical learning rather than theoretical discussion alone.

Participants will explore the complete process of developing a citizens’ assembly, from the initial concept through to implementation and follow-up.

1. Understanding Citizens’ Assemblies

The first stage will introduce participants to the concept of citizens’ assemblies and the principles that make them effective.

Participants will examine:

  • What citizens’ assemblies are
  • How they function
  • Their key democratic principles
  • Why deliberative approaches can complement traditional democratic processes
  • Examples of citizens’ assemblies in different European countries

Case studies from Ireland, France, Germany and other European contexts will be used to illustrate how deliberative processes have been applied in practice.

2. Planning a Citizens’ Assembly

Participants will learn about the important decisions that must be made before launching an assembly.

This includes:

  • Framing the question
  • Defining the purpose of the assembly
  • Establishing governance arrangements
  • Developing a recruitment approach
  • Considering the roles of different stakeholders
  • Preparing an appropriate structure for deliberation

Participants will also participate in group work where they begin drafting their own citizens’ assembly proposal.

This makes the workshop particularly relevant to people who already have an idea for a deliberative process in their municipality, organisation, region or community.

3. Moving From Planning to Practice

The second seminar day will focus on what happens after the initial planning stage.

Participants will explore the “in-between” phase of a citizens’ assembly, including:

  • Providing participants with information
  • Supporting deliberation
  • Facilitation
  • Developing recommendations
  • Following up on recommendations
  • Connecting citizens’ assemblies with public administration
  • Addressing local and regional considerations

Participants will then work on finalising their proposed citizens’ assemblies and presenting them for feedback.

4. Local and Regional Democracy

A major focus of the workshop is the application of deliberative democracy at the local and regional level.

This is particularly relevant to:

  • Municipal officials
  • Local government representatives
  • Regional authorities
  • Youth-policy professionals
  • Civil society organisations
  • Community advocates

The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities will contribute expertise on embedding deliberative processes within municipal and regional governance.

This can help participants understand how citizens’ assemblies can move from an interesting democratic concept into a practical mechanism that can operate within existing institutions.

Public Panel Discussion on Deliberative Democracy

In addition to the two-day capacity-building workshop, participants will attend a high-level public panel discussion.

The panel will bring together international and Hungarian experts and will be open to diplomatic, civil society, academic and municipal stakeholders.

The discussion will address two broad areas:

  1. International evidence on citizens’ assemblies
  2. Citizens’ assemblies at the local level, including opportunities and how to get started

For workshop participants, the panel will provide direct expert input that can inform the practical training sessions that follow.

Who Can Apply?

The official call identifies several categories of people who are particularly encouraged to apply.

Young Activists and Civil Society Representatives

Young people actively involved in:

  • Democratic participation
  • Youth organisations
  • Civic advocacy
  • Community engagement
  • Democratic resilience
  • Civil society initiatives

may find the workshop particularly relevant.

Local and Regional Government Representatives

The programme also welcomes representatives of local and regional authorities who have responsibilities relating to:

  • Citizen engagement
  • Youth policy
  • Democratic innovation
  • Public participation
  • Local governance

These participants can potentially use the knowledge gained to introduce or strengthen participatory processes within their municipalities or regions.

Youth Centre and Civil Society Organisation Staff

Staff members working in youth centres and civil society organisations can also apply, particularly where their work involves democratic participation, civic education or participatory methodologies.

Political Education Practitioners

Staff of schools and organisations involved in political education who have an interest in participatory methods are also specifically included in the target group.

People With an Existing Citizens’ Assembly Idea

The opportunity is especially relevant to individuals who already have a concrete idea or project underway involving a citizens’ assembly or another deliberative process.

The idea could relate to:

  • A municipality
  • A region
  • A civil society organisation
  • A youth organisation
  • A community initiative
  • Another relevant institution

Having a concrete idea can help participants directly apply the workshop’s practical learning to their own context.

Eligibility Requirements

The official call specifies several important eligibility conditions.

Minimum Age

Applicants must be at least 18 years old.

Citizenship

Applicants must be citizens of a Council of Europe member state.

This is an important requirement. The opportunity is therefore not open globally to applicants from every country.

English Language

The workshop will be conducted in English, and participants are expected to have a working level of English.

Applicants should therefore be comfortable participating in discussions, group work, presentations and other interactive activities in English.

Interest and Motivation

Applicants should be motivated to bring citizens’ assemblies or deliberative democracy processes into their own contexts.

The programme is not simply looking for people who want to learn about democracy in general. It is specifically seeking people who can potentially use and apply the knowledge gained from the workshop.

What Are the Benefits of Participating?

The workshop provides several substantial benefits for selected participants.

Practical Expert-Led Training

Participants will receive two full days of practical, expert-led training focused on designing, planning and delivering citizens’ assemblies.

Rather than only studying deliberative democracy conceptually, participants will work through practical steps that can be applied in their own communities and organisations.

International Expert Exposure

Participants will gain access to a high-level public panel featuring international and Hungarian experts working on deliberative democracy.

This can provide insight into different approaches and experiences from across Europe.

Local and Regional Governance Knowledge

Participants will receive dedicated input from the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities on how deliberative processes can be integrated into municipal and regional governance.

Development of a Practical Proposal

A particularly valuable component is the structured group work.

Participants will develop a citizens’ assembly proposal that is tailored to their own organisation or community and receive expert feedback on their work.

This means participants can potentially leave Budapest with a much clearer roadmap for implementing a deliberative process.

European Networking

The programme will connect participants with a growing European network of people working on deliberative democracy.

This can provide opportunities for:

  • Knowledge exchange
  • Professional networking
  • Collaboration
  • Sharing experiences
  • Learning from other European contexts
  • Future democratic participation initiatives

Travel, Accommodation and Meals Covered

One of the most significant benefits is that travel, accommodation and meals are fully covered for selected participants, in accordance with Council of Europe rules.

Participants will be hosted at the European Youth Centre Budapest during the programme.

This makes the opportunity particularly attractive to eligible applicants who may otherwise find international training in Europe financially difficult to attend.

Programme Schedule

The official programme includes arrival, two main training days, a public panel discussion and departure.

Sunday, 18 October 2026 — Arrival

Participants are expected to arrive in Budapest on the evening of Sunday, 18 October 2026.

Activities include:

  • Registration
  • Welcome dinner

Participants will be hosted at the European Youth Centre Budapest.

Monday, 19 October 2026 — Seminar Day 1

The first seminar day focuses on:

What are citizens’ assemblies and how do you build one?

Key activities include:

  • Introduction to citizens’ assemblies
  • Key principles
  • Case studies from Ireland, France, Germany and other European contexts
  • Question framing
  • Governance
  • Recruitment
  • Group work
  • Beginning to draft a citizens’ assembly proposal

Tuesday, 20 October 2026 — Seminar Day 2

The second seminar focuses on:

From planning to practice

Participants will explore:

  • Information
  • Facilitation
  • Recommendations
  • Follow-up
  • Connecting with administration
  • Local and regional dimensions
  • Finalising citizens’ assembly proposals
  • Presenting proposals
  • Next steps

Tuesday, 20 October 2026 — Public Panel

The same day will also feature the public panel discussion on deliberative democracy.

The panel will examine international evidence and the practical opportunities for establishing citizens’ assemblies at the local level.

Wednesday, 21 October 2026 — Departure

An optional informal morning session will take place before departures beginning from 11:00 AM.

Participants are expected to depart on Wednesday, 21 October.

Application Process

Applicants must complete the official online application form before the deadline.

The application requires applicants to provide information that allows the organisers to understand their background, experience and motivation.

Applicants will be asked for:

  1. Name
  2. Age
  3. Country of residence
  4. Organisational affiliation
  5. A short description of their current work or engagement in democratic participation
  6. A statement explaining what they hope to gain from the workshop
  7. An explanation of how they would apply the knowledge gained in their work or community

The description of current work or engagement has a maximum length of 200 words.

The statement about what the applicant hopes to gain and how they will apply the learning also has a maximum length of 200 words.

How to Write a Strong Application

Because approximately 30 participants are expected to be selected, applicants should make their responses clear, specific and relevant.

A strong application should demonstrate more than a general interest in democracy.

Applicants should consider highlighting:

Relevant Experience

Explain your current involvement in:

  • Youth participation
  • Civic engagement
  • Civil society
  • Local government
  • Democratic innovation
  • Political education
  • Community development
  • Participatory decision-making

A Concrete Idea

If you already have an idea for a citizens’ assembly, explain it clearly.

For example, you could describe:

  • The issue you want citizens to deliberate on
  • The community or municipality involved
  • Why the issue requires citizen participation
  • What you hope the assembly could achieve

Practical Application

Explain what you intend to do with the knowledge gained after returning home.

This is important because the programme is intended to create practical capacity for deliberative democracy rather than simply provide theoretical knowledge.

Selection Considerations

The organisers expect approximately 30 participants to be selected.

Geographic diversity is specifically identified as an important selection criterion.

The organisers particularly encourage applications from Central and Eastern Europe.

However, applicants from other Council of Europe member states can also apply, provided they meet the eligibility conditions.

Important Dates

Applicants should keep the following dates in mind:

  • 10 August 2026: Call opens
  • 7 September 2026: Application deadline
  • 21 September 2026: Notification of results
  • 18 October 2026: Arrival in Budapest
  • 19–21 October 2026: Workshop
  • 21 October 2026: Departure

Applications received after 7 September 2026 will not be considered.

                         Learn more about this opportunity HERE

Where Will the Workshop Take Place?

The event will be held at the:

European Youth Centre Budapest

Budapest, Hungary

The European Youth Centre provides the setting for the Council of Europe’s youth-related educational and capacity-building activities.

Participants will be hosted at the centre throughout the workshop period.

Why This Opportunity Matters for Young People

Young people are important stakeholders in democratic decision-making, but traditional political systems do not always provide sufficient opportunities for young people to participate meaningfully in decisions affecting their communities.

Deliberative democracy offers another approach by creating structured opportunities for citizens to learn about issues, hear different perspectives, discuss possible solutions and develop recommendations.

For young activists and youth organisations, learning how to establish and facilitate citizens’ assemblies can therefore provide a practical tool for strengthening youth participation.

The workshop can also help participants understand how youth engagement can be connected to local and regional decision-making.

Final Checklist Before Applying

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should confirm that they:

  • Are at least 18 years old
  • Are a citizen of a Council of Europe member state
  • Have a working level of English
  • Are actively involved or interested in democratic participation
  • Fit one of the target participant profiles
  • Have a genuine interest in deliberative democracy
  • Ideally have a concrete citizens’ assembly or deliberative-process idea
  • Can explain how they will apply the training in their organisation or community
  • Can attend the workshop in Budapest from 19–21 October 2026
  • Can arrive on 18 October 2026
  • Submit the online application before 7 September 2026

                                                APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The Council of Europe Deliberative Democracy and Citizens’ Assemblies Workshop 2026 offers an excellent opportunity for eligible youth activists, civil society representatives, local and regional authorities, youth workers and democratic participation practitioners to develop practical skills in citizen engagement.

Rather than focusing exclusively on theory, the workshop will teach participants how to move from the idea of a citizens’ assembly to practical planning and implementation. Participants will explore real European examples, develop their own proposals, receive expert feedback and learn how deliberative processes can be integrated into local and regional governance.

The opportunity is also particularly valuable financially because selected participants will receive full coverage of travel, accommodation and meals, in accordance with Council of Europe rules.

Eligible applicants should prepare their applications carefully and clearly demonstrate their current involvement in democratic participation, their motivation for attending and how they intend to use the knowledge gained in their own organisation or community.

item.content:encoded:
The DIEM Project (Developing Inclusive Education in the Mediterranean) has officially launched its Call for Applications for the International Training of Trainers (ToT) Programme, a specialised international capacity-building opportunity for professionals, researchers, academics and institutional representatives working in the field of Cultural Heritage.

The programme is designed to strengthen participants’ professional knowledge, practical competencies and international networks in areas such as Cultural Heritage management, conservation, documentation, governance and communication. It will combine online theoretical learning, practical online training and an international workshop in Jordan.

Applications are currently open, and interested candidates are encouraged to submit their applications before the stated deadline.

DIEM International Training of Trainers Programme 2026 at a Glance

  • Programme: DIEM International Training of Trainers (ToT) Programme
  • Project: Developing Inclusive Education in the Mediterranean (DIEM)
  • Field: Cultural Heritage
  • Training format: Online training plus an international workshop
  • Training language: English
  • Total online training: 40 hours
  • International workshop: Jordan
  • Workshop duration: 4–5 days
  • Expected workshop period: Early 2027
  • Application deadline: 31 August 2026
  • Travel and accommodation: Covered for selected participants, subject to the DIEM Project’s applicable rules
  • Application method: Online application form

The DIEM project is an international initiative focused on strengthening education, skills development and employment opportunities connected to Cultural Heritage across the Mediterranean. The wider project involves six countries: Italy, Egypt, Jordan, Tunisia, Spain and Palestine.

What Is the DIEM International Training of Trainers Programme?

The International Training of Trainers Programme is a capacity-building component of the DIEM project aimed at developing a group of professionals and academic or institutional actors who can contribute to stronger Cultural Heritage education and management.

Cultural Heritage sites require professionals who understand not only preservation and conservation, but also how heritage can be documented, managed, communicated and integrated into broader educational and development strategies.

The DIEM ToT programme therefore takes a comprehensive approach. Participants will be exposed to theoretical knowledge, practical methodologies, international best practices and collaborative activities that can help them develop or improve management and communication plans for selected heritage sites.

The programme also contributes to DIEM’s broader cascade-training approach. The project plans to train 85 site managers and professors in Group A, who can subsequently contribute to training other target groups within the project.

Who Is the Programme Designed For?

The call specifically targets people with professional, academic or institutional involvement in Cultural Heritage.

Potential applicants include:

  • Heritage site managers
  • Museum managers
  • Representatives of public institutions
  • University professors
  • Researchers
  • Cultural Heritage professionals

The programme is therefore not presented as a general course for anyone interested in history or culture. It is aimed at individuals who already have a professional, academic or institutional connection to Cultural Heritage and can potentially use the knowledge gained through the programme in their organisations, institutions, heritage sites or educational activities.

Key Areas Covered by the Training

The programme will provide participants with knowledge and practical exposure across several important Cultural Heritage disciplines.

1. Cultural Heritage Management

Participants will explore approaches to managing Cultural Heritage resources and sites in a sustainable and effective manner.

Heritage management involves balancing preservation with education, public engagement, institutional responsibilities and the long-term sustainability of heritage assets.

2. Conservation

The training will introduce participants to important principles and approaches related to the conservation of Cultural Heritage.

This area is particularly relevant to professionals responsible for protecting heritage assets from deterioration, inappropriate intervention and other threats.

3. Documentation

Proper documentation is fundamental to Cultural Heritage management.

The programme will address documentation as part of the wider process of understanding, recording and managing heritage resources. Strong documentation can support decision-making, conservation planning, research, communication and future management activities.

4. Governance

The programme will also examine Cultural Heritage governance and the role of institutions and stakeholders in managing heritage resources.

Effective governance can involve cooperation between public institutions, academic organisations, heritage professionals, local communities and other relevant stakeholders.

5. International Best Practices

Participants will have the opportunity to learn from international experts and approaches to Cultural Heritage management.

This international perspective is an important component of the programme because it allows participants to compare experiences, exchange knowledge and understand how different approaches can be adapted to their own professional contexts.

Structure of the DIEM Training Programme

The programme will be delivered through three main phases, combining online learning with an international practical workshop.

Phase 1: Theoretical Online Training

The first phase will consist of 20 hours of online theoretical training, scheduled to begin from mid-September 2026.

The sessions will be delivered in English by international experts.

The theoretical component is expected to provide participants with a common foundation before they progress to the more practical elements of the programme.

Key areas include:

  • Cultural Heritage management
  • Conservation
  • Documentation
  • Governance
  • International best practices

Participants will therefore begin by developing and strengthening their theoretical understanding of the key concepts that underpin effective Cultural Heritage management.

Phase 2: Applied Online Training

The second phase will consist of another 20 hours of online training, expected to begin from mid-October 2026.

Unlike the first phase, this component will place greater emphasis on application and interaction.

Participants will work through practical sessions designed to support the development of Management and Communication Plans for selected Cultural Heritage pilot sites.

This applied component is particularly important because it gives participants an opportunity to move beyond theoretical knowledge and consider how the concepts learned during the programme can be translated into practical planning.

The training can therefore help participants develop skills in areas such as:

  • Planning for Cultural Heritage sites
  • Developing management approaches
  • Preparing communication strategies
  • Applying professional knowledge to real heritage contexts
  • Working collaboratively with other professionals
  • Sharing and evaluating different approaches

Phase 3: International Workshop in Jordan

The third phase will take participants beyond the online learning environment.

Selected participants will attend an international workshop in Jordan, expected to take place for approximately 4–5 days in early 2027.

The Jordan workshop will provide an opportunity for participants to work directly with DIEM experts and other participants in an international environment.

During the workshop, selected participants are expected to:

  • Work with DIEM experts on pilot-site Management and Communication Plans
  • Participate in practical activities
  • Contribute to the development of the Groups B and C Training Toolkit
  • Exchange knowledge and experiences with participants from other contexts
  • Strengthen international professional cooperation
  • Apply knowledge acquired during the online training

One of the significant advantages of this component is the opportunity for practical and international exposure.

Travel and Accommodation Support

For participants selected to attend the international workshop in Jordan, the DIEM Project will cover travel and accommodation costs, subject to the project’s applicable rules.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the official participation conditions and ToT Syllabus before applying because the coverage is stated as being subject to project rules.

Training Language and Accessibility

The entire online training programme will be delivered in English.

This means that applicants should be prepared to participate in English-language lectures, discussions and practical activities.

The programme will also provide additional accessibility measures.

Recordings of lectures will be made available after each session through the DIEM digital platform. In addition, subtitles in the languages of the project partners are planned to support wider accessibility and participation.

This can be particularly useful for participants who may not be able to attend every live online session or who want to revisit particular training materials.

Why This Programme Is Important

Cultural Heritage is not only about preserving historical buildings, monuments, museums or archaeological sites. Effective heritage management also involves education, communication, documentation, governance, community engagement and sustainable development.

The DIEM project recognises the need to strengthen these skills across the Mediterranean.

According to the project, DIEM seeks to address the gap between the region’s rich Cultural Heritage and limited access to inclusive education and employment opportunities. Its broader activities include training Cultural Heritage professionals, supporting humanities graduates and developing skills among vulnerable groups.

The project also seeks to create a cooperative model for Cultural Heritage education and professional development across participating countries.

International Networking and Knowledge Exchange

Another important feature of the ToT programme is its international dimension.

Participants will come into contact with professionals, researchers, academics and institutional representatives working within different Cultural Heritage environments.

This can create opportunities for:

  • International knowledge exchange
  • Professional networking
  • Sharing Cultural Heritage management experiences
  • Learning from different institutional approaches
  • Developing international collaborations
  • Understanding Cultural Heritage challenges from a Mediterranean perspective

The wider DIEM project involves partners from Italy, Egypt, Jordan, Tunisia, Spain and Palestine, creating a cross-country network connecting Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

How the Programme Connects to the Wider DIEM Project

The ToT programme is part of a broader DIEM strategy rather than an isolated training course.

The project plans to develop a cascade model in which trained professionals and academics can contribute to the development of further training activities.

According to DIEM’s project information, the wider initiative includes:

  1. Training 85 site managers and professors as Group A.
  2. Providing cascade training for 110 unemployed humanities graduates as Group B.
  3. Developing skills among 560 vulnerable individuals, including women, NEETs and rural youth, through Group C activities.
  4. Developing multilingual e-learning resources and an inclusion strategy.
  5. Creating management plans and communication strategies for 10 pilot Cultural Heritage sites.
  6. Strengthening cooperation among public authorities, municipalities, universities, research centres, cultural enterprises and other stakeholders.

This means that the ToT programme has a potential multiplier effect: participants are not only expected to gain knowledge for their own professional development but can become part of a wider system for transferring Cultural Heritage knowledge and skills.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The programme may be particularly relevant to professionals who are already involved in:

  • Managing museums or heritage sites
  • Cultural Heritage research
  • Heritage conservation
  • University teaching and academic research
  • Public-sector Cultural Heritage administration
  • Cultural Heritage documentation
  • Heritage communication
  • Cultural Heritage education and training
  • Institutional management of Cultural Heritage resources

Applicants should consider whether they can actively participate in the full training process, including the online components and, if selected, the international workshop in Jordan.

Geographical Scope of the Opportunity

The DIEM project operates across six participating countries:

  • Italy
  • Spain
  • Egypt
  • Tunisia
  • Jordan
  • Palestine

These countries span three geographical regions/continents: Europe, Africa and Asia. Italy and Spain are in Europe; Egypt and Tunisia are in Africa; while Jordan and Palestine are in Asia.

The official DIEM project information identifies these six countries as the countries involved in the project.

Applicants should therefore consult the official ToT Syllabus and application requirements carefully to confirm the precise eligibility conditions applicable to individual applicants before submitting an application.

Application Process

Interested candidates are required to complete the official online application form.

The application should be submitted electronically through the designated application platform.

Candidates should ensure that they carefully review the eligibility requirements, selection criteria, training structure and participation conditions before submitting their application.

                                                      APPLY HERE

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications is:

31 August 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day to submit their applications. Completing the application early allows candidates sufficient time to review their information, correct errors and ensure that all required sections have been completed.

Important Dates

The programme follows a multi-stage schedule:

  • 31 August 2026: Application deadline
  • Mid-September 2026: Phase 1 theoretical online training begins
  • Mid-October 2026: Phase 2 applied online training begins
  • Early 2027: International workshop in Jordan
  • International workshop duration: Approximately 4–5 days

These dates are based on the published call and may be subject to adjustments by the DIEM Project.

Tips for Applicants

Applicants can strengthen their preparation by making sure their application clearly demonstrates their connection to Cultural Heritage.

Before submitting, candidates should:

  1. Clearly explain their current professional, academic or institutional role.
  2. Highlight relevant experience in Cultural Heritage.
  3. Demonstrate why the training is relevant to their work.
  4. Show how they intend to apply the knowledge gained from the programme.
  5. Carefully review the official eligibility requirements.
  6. Ensure that the application is completed in English where required.
  7. Review the ToT Syllabus before submitting the application.
  8. Submit the application before 31 August 2026.

What Participants Can Gain From the Programme

The programme offers participants an opportunity to strengthen both technical knowledge and international professional exposure.

Participants can expect to develop or improve their understanding of:

  • Cultural Heritage management
  • Conservation approaches
  • Heritage documentation
  • Governance
  • Communication and management planning
  • International Cultural Heritage practices
  • Training and knowledge-transfer approaches
  • International cooperation and networking

The practical work can also provide participants with experience in developing Management and Communication Plans for heritage sites.

                   Learn more about this opportunity HERE

Conclusion

The DIEM International Training of Trainers Programme 2026 is a significant professional development opportunity for Cultural Heritage managers, museum professionals, university professors, researchers, public institution representatives and other professionals working in the heritage sector.

With 40 hours of online training, international expert-led sessions, applied learning, access to recorded lectures, practical work on Cultural Heritage management and communication plans, and an international workshop in Jordan, the programme provides a combination of theoretical learning, practical application and international knowledge exchange.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to professionals who want to strengthen their Cultural Heritage expertise while connecting with colleagues and institutions across the Mediterranean.

Eligible and interested candidates should carefully review the official programme information and submit their applications before the 31 August 2026 deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC), with funding from the Caribbean Development Bank, has opened applications for the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship, an opportunity designed to support emerging Caribbean professionals working or interested in climate change, sustainable development and public engagement.

The fellowship will give two young Caribbean professionals the opportunity to attend UNFCCC COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as part of the CCCCC delegation. Selected fellows will receive funding covering return travel, accommodation and a daily per diem, while also receiving official observer access to the COP31 Blue Zone.

Beyond attending an international climate conference, the fellowship is structured as a regional capacity-building experience. Fellows will participate in activities before, during and after COP31, gaining exposure to international climate negotiations, regional climate priorities and professional networks that can be used to strengthen climate action across the Caribbean.

Application deadline: 21 August 2026.

Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026 at a Glance

Opportunity Details
Fellowship Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship
Organiser Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC)
Funding partner Caribbean Development Bank
Conference UNFCCC COP31
Location Antalya, Türkiye
COP31 dates 9–20 November 2026
Number of fellows 2
Age requirement 18–30
Eligibility Nationals of CARICOM Member States
Funding Fully funded
Travel Return economy airfare
Accommodation Hotel accommodation
Living support Daily per diem
COP access Blue Zone observer accreditation
Application deadline 21 August 2026

What Is the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship?

The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship is a professional development initiative created to help develop the next generation of Caribbean climate professionals.

The programme recognises that international climate negotiations can have significant consequences for Caribbean countries, particularly Small Island Developing States that face challenges related to climate adaptation, climate finance, loss and damage and the Global Goal on Adaptation.

Through participation in COP31, fellows will have the opportunity to gain first-hand exposure to the international climate policy process while learning about the role of the CCCCC in coordinating regional climate action.

The fellowship is therefore not simply an opportunity to attend COP31. It is designed to help participants understand, contribute to and communicate the climate agenda affecting the Caribbean.

Why COP31 Matters to the Caribbean

COP31 will bring together governments, climate experts, development partners, advocates and other stakeholders from around the world to discuss international climate action.

For Caribbean countries, international climate negotiations are particularly important because climate-related decisions can directly influence the region’s ability to respond to climate risks.

Among the issues particularly relevant to Caribbean countries are:

  • Climate adaptation
  • Climate finance
  • Loss and damage
  • The Global Goal on Adaptation
  • Sustainable development
  • Climate resilience
  • International cooperation
  • Support for Small Island Developing States

The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship aims to equip young professionals with the knowledge and experience needed to understand these discussions and contribute to the region’s climate agenda.

What Will Fellows Experience?

Selected fellows will participate in the full fellowship cycle, beginning before COP31 and continuing after the conference.

The programme has three broad stages:

1. Pre-COP Preparation

Before travelling to Türkiye, fellows will participate in preparation activities designed to help them understand their role and maximise their contribution to COP31.

This preparation can include:

  • Professional development
  • Understanding the UNFCCC process
  • Defining the fellow’s role during COP31
  • Preparing for participation in the CCCCC delegation
  • Understanding Caribbean climate priorities
  • Preparing for knowledge-sharing activities

This preparation is intended to ensure that fellows arrive at COP31 ready to participate meaningfully rather than simply attend the conference.

2. Participation During COP31

Fellows will join the CCCCC delegation during COP31 in Antalya.

They will have access to the official Blue Zone as observers through the CCCCC delegation quota.

This provides an opportunity to experience an important part of the international climate process and attend activities accessible to observers.

Fellows may be able to participate in:

  • Plenary sessions
  • Observer-accessible sessions
  • Side events
  • Activities at the CARICOM Pavilion
  • Other relevant COP31 activities

3. Post-COP Knowledge Transfer

The fellowship does not end when COP31 concludes.

Participants will be expected to contribute to post-conference knowledge-sharing activities across the Caribbean.

This means fellows will have an opportunity to take the knowledge, insights and connections developed during COP31 and share them with their organisations, communities and wider Caribbean audiences.

What Does the Fellowship Cover?

The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship is described as fully funded.

The funding package includes several major costs associated with participating in COP31.

Return Airfare

Selected fellows will receive economy-class return airfare from their home country to Antalya, Türkiye.

This removes one of the biggest financial barriers associated with international conference participation.

Accommodation

The fellowship provides hotel accommodation throughout the conference period.

Fellows therefore do not need to independently finance their conference-period accommodation.

Daily Per Diem

Participants will receive a daily allowance to cover meals and incidental expenses during the fellowship.

This provides additional financial support while fellows are participating in COP31.

Blue Zone Observer Accreditation

Selected fellows will receive official Blue Zone observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation quota.

This is an important component of the opportunity because it provides access to COP31 activities available to accredited observers.

Mentorship

Fellows will receive guidance from experienced members of the CCCCC delegation.

Mentorship will take place:

  • Before COP31
  • During COP31
  • After COP31

This can help participants better understand the international climate process and make the most of their experience.

Professional Development

The fellowship also includes structured professional development through:

  • Pre-COP preparation
  • Role definition
  • COP31 participation
  • Post-conference knowledge-sharing
  • Exposure to experienced climate professionals
  • Regional and international networking

Who Can Apply for the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship?

The fellowship is specifically designed for young Caribbean professionals between 18 and 30 years old.

Applicants should be early-career, mid-career or emerging professionals with a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development.

However, applicants must meet several specific eligibility requirements.

1. Age Requirement

Applicants must be between 18 and 30 years old.

This makes the fellowship particularly relevant to young professionals and emerging leaders who are beginning to establish careers in climate action, development, communications, public engagement or related areas.

2. Citizenship Requirement

Applicants must be nationals of a CARICOM Member State.

This is a key eligibility condition.

The fellowship is specifically designed to strengthen Caribbean climate leadership, meaning applicants from countries outside the CARICOM membership framework do not qualify simply because they work on climate-related issues.

3. Caribbean-Based Organisation Affiliation

Applicants must be affiliated with or work with a Caribbean-based organisation.

The organisation may fall into a number of categories, including:

  • Youth organisations
  • Non-governmental organisations
  • Community-based organisations
  • Private-sector organisations
  • Public-sector institutions
  • Other organisations working in climate, development or public engagement

4. Education, Employment or Organisational Involvement

Applicants should currently be:

  • Enrolled in tertiary education;
  • Employed; or
  • Actively involved with a relevant organisation.

Their work, studies or involvement should connect to climate change, development, public engagement or related areas.

5. Climate and Sustainable Development Interest

Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development.

The programme is intended for people who can contribute to the Caribbean’s climate agenda and eventually help translate international climate discussions into meaningful regional action.

6. Cannot Be an Official Party Negotiator

Applicants must not currently be serving as an official Party negotiator.

The fellowship is aimed at emerging professionals who will participate through the CCCCC delegation rather than individuals already serving as official government negotiators in the UNFCCC process.

What Organisations Can Applicants Come From?

The fellowship is open to individuals connected to a range of organisations.

Potential applicants may be affiliated with:

Youth Organisations

Young people involved in youth-led initiatives and organisations can apply if they meet the other requirements.

Non-Governmental Organisations

Professionals and emerging leaders working with NGOs on climate, development, advocacy or related issues may be eligible.

Community-Based Organisations

Applicants involved in community-level climate or development initiatives may also qualify.

Private-Sector Organisations

Young professionals working in businesses or other private-sector organisations can apply where their work or interests align with the fellowship requirements.

Public-Sector Institutions

Applicants working in government or public institutions can also be eligible, provided they meet the requirements and are not serving as official Party negotiators.

Other Relevant Organisations

The fellowship also recognises organisations working in areas such as:

  • Climate action
  • Sustainable development
  • Public engagement
  • Environmental issues
  • Community development
  • Related areas of regional importance

The Blue Zone Access Explained

One of the most valuable features of the fellowship is access to the COP31 Blue Zone.

Selected fellows will receive observer accreditation through the CCCCC’s available quota.

This means fellows who are selected can attend activities accessible to accredited observers, including relevant plenaries, sessions, side events and activities at the CARICOM Pavilion.

The fellowship also encourages participants to explore accreditation through their respective national delegations.

National delegation accreditation could potentially provide additional opportunities to observe negotiation processes and contribute to country delegations where appropriate.

However, this additional accreditation is not guaranteed.

The decision to provide accreditation through a national government rests entirely with the relevant government.

The CCCCC may provide a supporting letter to the appropriate government upon request, but this does not guarantee national delegation accreditation.

Importantly, a fellow who does not receive national delegation accreditation can still participate through their Blue Zone observer accreditation provided via the CCCCC delegation.

Application Requirements

Applicants need to prepare several important materials before applying.

1. Current Curriculum Vitae

Applicants must provide a current CV.

The CV should clearly demonstrate relevant aspects of the applicant’s background, including:

  • Education
  • Professional experience
  • Volunteer involvement
  • Climate-related work
  • Relevant skills
  • Organisational involvement

Applicants should make sure their CV clearly communicates their connection to climate action, sustainable development, public engagement or other relevant areas.

APPLY HERE.

2. Written Application of 1,200–1,500 Words

Applicants must submit a written application between 1,200 and 1,500 words.

The application must address three major areas.

Professional Development

Applicants should explain how participation in the fellowship would contribute to their professional development.

This section should address:

  • Skills they expect to develop
  • Knowledge they hope to gain
  • Experience they want to acquire
  • Their career trajectory
  • Why this is the right time for them to participate

Applicants should demonstrate that they have thought carefully about how the fellowship fits into their professional journey.

Institutional Impact

Applicants should explain how their participation would benefit their organisation or institution.

They should provide a realistic plan explaining how they intend to share:

  • Knowledge
  • Insights
  • Lessons from COP31
  • Professional networks
  • Relevant climate information

with their colleagues, organisation or community.

A strong answer should demonstrate that the benefits of the fellowship will extend beyond the individual participant.

Caribbean Climate Literacy

Applicants must explain how their COP31 experience will help translate complex climate discussions into accessible information for Caribbean audiences.

The goal is to demonstrate how the applicant can contribute to stronger climate literacy and public engagement across the Caribbean.

A short supporting statement from the applicant’s organisation or institution is encouraged.

How Will Applications Be Assessed?

Applications will primarily be assessed according to the strength, clarity and credibility of the three required written statements.

The selection panel will give particular consideration to several factors.

Commitment to the Caribbean Climate Agenda

Applicants should demonstrate genuine interest in the climate issues affecting Caribbean countries and the wider region.

Professional Value

The selection panel will consider how valuable the fellowship would be to the applicant’s professional development.

Applicants should therefore explain why participation at this particular stage of their career would make a meaningful difference.

Institutional Knowledge Transfer

Applicants need to present a credible plan for transferring the knowledge and insights gained through COP31 to their organisation or community.

Climate Literacy Contribution

The panel will assess how effectively applicants can help make climate discussions understandable and accessible to Caribbean communities.

Communication Skills

Applicants should demonstrate an ability to communicate climate information effectively.

This is particularly important because fellows are expected to help translate international climate discussions into accessible information.

Potential Impact Beyond COP31

The selection process will also consider whether the fellowship could produce meaningful impact after the conference.

The ideal candidate will not simply benefit personally from attending COP31 but will use the experience to contribute to wider Caribbean climate action.

Interview and Final Selection

After applications have been reviewed, shortlisted candidates will be invited to an interview with a CCCCC selection panel.

Following the selection process, only two fellows will be selected.

Because there are only two fellowship positions, applicants should ensure that their application clearly communicates their motivation, experience, potential impact and connection to the Caribbean climate agenda.

For more information VISIT HERE.

Important Dates

Applicants should take note of the following dates:

Applications open: 10 August 2026

Application deadline: 21 August 2026

COP31: 9–20 November 2026

Location: Antalya, Türkiye

Only a short period is available between the opening of applications and the deadline, so eligible applicants should begin preparing their CV and written application as early as possible.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants can take several steps to make their application more compelling.

Research Caribbean Climate Priorities

Develop a clear understanding of the climate challenges facing Caribbean countries and the importance of issues such as adaptation, climate finance, loss and damage and climate resilience.

Connect COP31 to Your Career

Do not simply state that attending COP31 would be valuable.

Explain exactly how the experience would support your professional goals and the skills you want to develop.

Present a Realistic Knowledge-Sharing Plan

The fellowship places significant emphasis on institutional impact.

Think about what you would actually do after COP31 to share your knowledge.

For example, you could consider activities such as:

  • Internal presentations
  • Community discussions
  • Educational content
  • Workshops
  • Social media campaigns
  • Articles
  • Youth engagement activities
  • Climate literacy initiatives

Demonstrate Communication Ability

Since climate literacy is an important part of the fellowship, applicants should demonstrate their ability to communicate complex subjects in ways that ordinary audiences can understand.

Show Regional Commitment

Explain how your experience, interests or work connects with the needs and priorities of Caribbean communities.

Proofread the Written Application

The written component has a specific 1,200–1,500-word requirement.

Applicants should ensure their submission remains within the required range while answering all three areas fully.

Why This Fellowship Is a Valuable Opportunity

The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship combines international exposure, professional development, mentorship and practical climate engagement.

Selected fellows will have the opportunity to:

  • Attend COP31 in Türkiye.
  • Receive fully funded return economy airfare.
  • Receive accommodation during the conference period.
  • Receive a daily per diem.
  • Obtain Blue Zone observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation.
  • Receive mentorship from experienced climate professionals.
  • Learn more about the UNFCCC process.
  • Develop professional skills.
  • Build international and regional networks.
  • Learn more about Caribbean climate priorities.
  • Participate in COP31-related activities.
  • Share knowledge with organisations and communities after the conference.
  • Contribute to stronger climate literacy across the Caribbean.

The fellowship therefore has the potential to benefit both the selected individuals and the wider organisations and communities they represent.

A Platform for the Next Generation of Caribbean Climate Leaders

Climate change presents significant challenges for Caribbean countries, particularly because many countries in the region are vulnerable to climate impacts despite contributing relatively little to global emissions.

Developing professionals who understand international climate negotiations and can communicate climate issues effectively is therefore important for the region’s future.

The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship seeks to contribute to this effort by giving emerging professionals direct exposure to COP31 while preparing them to take the knowledge gained back to their communities.

The programme’s emphasis on knowledge transfer is particularly significant. Fellows are expected to help ensure that their experience benefits more than just themselves.

Conclusion

The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026 offers two young Caribbean professionals the opportunity to experience UNFCCC COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, while developing professional skills, building networks and contributing to the Caribbean’s climate agenda.

The fellowship is fully funded, covering return economy airfare, accommodation and a daily per diem. Selected fellows will also receive Blue Zone observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation and mentorship before, during and after COP31.

Applicants must be 18–30 years old, nationals of a CARICOM Member State and affiliated with or working with a Caribbean-based organisation. They should have a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development and must not currently be serving as official Party negotiators.

The application requires a current CV and a 1,200–1,500-word written application addressing professional development, institutional impact and Caribbean climate literacy.

With only two fellows to be selected, applicants should focus on demonstrating their commitment to the Caribbean climate agenda, their ability to communicate climate information and their potential to create impact beyond COP31.

Application deadline: 21 August 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research (LIVES) has opened applications for its next cohort of doctoral researchers, offering early-stage PhD candidates the opportunity to join an internationally oriented and interdisciplinary doctoral programme focused on life course and lifespan research.

The LIVES Doctoral Programme is designed for researchers whose doctoral projects examine how people’s lives develop and change over time, including issues surrounding education, employment, health, ageing, social transitions, family experiences, public policy, and other factors that influence individual and collective life trajectories.

The programme has been running since 2012 and has supported more than 130 PhD graduates. For the upcoming cohort, LIVES is inviting applications from eligible doctoral students who want to strengthen their theoretical knowledge, methodological expertise, interdisciplinary research skills, and academic networks.

The new cohort will run from December 2026 to February 2029, with activities taking place at the University of Geneva and the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

Opportunity Overview

The LIVES Doctoral Programme provides structured doctoral training for PhD candidates whose research is connected to the study of life courses and human development across time.

Rather than being a conventional PhD scholarship or a standalone doctoral degree, the programme functions as an additional specialised training programme that doctoral candidates can undertake alongside their existing disciplinary PhD training.

This makes it particularly valuable for researchers who are already enrolled in doctoral programmes and want to develop stronger expertise in life course theory, longitudinal research, interdisciplinary approaches, and advanced methodological techniques.

Key details at a glance

  • Programme: LIVES Doctoral Programme
  • Cohort: December 2026 – February 2029
  • Host: Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research (LIVES)
  • Locations: University of Geneva and University of Lausanne, Switzerland
  • Opportunity type: Doctoral training programme
  • Target applicants: Early-stage PhD/doctoral students
  • Research focus: Life course and lifespan research
  • Eligible fields: Social sciences, psychology, health sciences and related disciplines
  • Study/research format: In-person workshops, training sessions and academic events
  • English requirement: Minimum B2 level
  • Application deadline: 30 September 2026
  • Admissions decision: No later than the end of October 2026
  • Programme start: December 2026

What Is the LIVES Doctoral Programme?

The LIVES Doctoral Programme is a specialised interdisciplinary programme developed to support doctoral researchers studying life course processes.

The programme recognises that important outcomes in people’s lives are often shaped by events and experiences occurring at different points throughout their lives. Researchers may therefore need approaches that can connect childhood experiences, education, employment, health, family life, ageing, social change and other transitions across time.

LIVES brings together doctoral researchers working on these kinds of questions and provides them with opportunities to receive training from specialists, exchange ideas with other PhD candidates and obtain feedback from experienced researchers.

The programme also places considerable emphasis on longitudinal methods and life course analysis, making it particularly relevant to researchers working with data that follows people, groups or populations over extended periods.

Who Should Apply?

The programme is aimed at early-stage doctoral students whose PhD research has a clear life course or lifespan perspective.

Potential applicants may be researching a wide variety of topics. What matters most is the connection between the doctoral project and life course research.

Applicants may come from disciplines such as:

  • Sociology
  • Demography
  • Psychology
  • Epidemiology
  • Economics
  • Political Science
  • Neuroscience
  • History
  • Gender Studies
  • Health sciences
  • Other related disciplines

The programme is interdisciplinary, meaning that applicants do not necessarily need to come from one specific academic department.

Examples of Eligible Research Topics

LIVES provides several examples of research areas that can fit within its programme.

1. Early-Life Events and Later Outcomes

Research may investigate how experiences during childhood, adolescence or other early stages of life affect outcomes later in life.

For example, a doctoral researcher could study how childhood socioeconomic circumstances influence educational achievement, employment opportunities, health or social mobility later in adulthood.

2. Life Trajectories Across Different Domains

Applicants may study how people’s trajectories develop across different areas of life.

Possible domains include:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Health
  • Family
  • Social relationships
  • Economic circumstances
  • Migration
  • Ageing

Such research can examine how developments in one area of life interact with developments in another.

3. Turning Points and Transitions

Life course research can also focus on major transitions and turning points in individual biographies.

Examples could include:

  • Transition from school to work
  • Marriage or partnership
  • Parenthood
  • Retirement
  • Migration
  • Career changes
  • Major health events
  • Educational transitions

Researchers may investigate what causes these transitions and how they affect people’s subsequent trajectories.

4. Accumulation and Depletion Across the Life Span

The programme also welcomes research examining how advantages and disadvantages accumulate or diminish over time.

This could involve studying how socioeconomic advantage, educational opportunities, health conditions or social resources build up across different stages of life.

5. Longitudinal Methods and Data Analysis

Applicants whose projects involve longitudinal datasets and methods may find the programme particularly relevant.

Longitudinal research allows researchers to examine change over time rather than relying solely on observations from a single point.

6. Changing Social Norms Around Age and Ageing

Another potential area concerns changing attitudes, expectations and social norms surrounding age and ageing.

Researchers could examine how societies understand different stages of life and how these expectations change over generations.

7. Life Course Research and Public Policy

The programme also welcomes research examining how life course concepts can contribute to public policy.

This could include research into policies affecting education, employment, healthcare, ageing, family life, social protection or other areas of public policy.

Programme Structure

The LIVES Doctoral Programme is organised over approximately two years and combines theoretical training, methodological workshops, doctoral presentations and individual academic feedback.

Participants are expected to attend a number of activities throughout the programme.

The structure includes four intensive sessions on theories and concepts in life course research.

Each theoretical session lasts approximately two to three days and is designed to strengthen participants’ understanding of the conceptual foundations of life course research.

The programme also provides four methodological workshops focusing on longitudinal and life course analysis.

These workshops last approximately two to four days and are intended to develop participants’ ability to apply appropriate methods to life course research.

LIVES Doctoriales

A particularly important part of the programme is the LIVES Doctoriales.

Two annual Doctoriales are organised during the programme. These provide PhD candidates with an opportunity to present their research to senior scholars and receive expert feedback.

Presenting doctoral research in this setting can help researchers identify weaknesses, refine research questions, improve theoretical frameworks and strengthen methodological approaches.

It also provides valuable experience in communicating academic research to an expert audience.

Individual Expert Feedback

Participants also receive an individual feedback session.

During this session, doctoral researchers have the opportunity to discuss and exchange ideas about their research with an invited expert.

This personalised academic interaction can be particularly useful when a researcher is trying to address a difficult theoretical, methodological or conceptual issue within their thesis.

Commitment Required from Participants

Applicants should understand that joining the LIVES Doctoral Programme requires an active commitment to participation.

Participants are expected to attend at least 13 days of their choice from the eight doctoral workshops.

The programme also identifies certain activities as compulsory.

According to the call, Session 1 and the two LIVES Doctoriales are compulsory, and selected workshops and Doctoriales must be attended in person.

The programme is designed to complement, rather than replace, a participant’s existing disciplinary doctoral training.

PhD candidates who want to undertake LIVES training alongside their disciplinary training are explicitly welcome.

For example, a doctoral researcher may continue specialised training in areas such as social psychology, neuroscience or another discipline while participating in the LIVES programme.

Certificates and ECTS Credits

Participants can receive certificates of attendance for the programme modules.

The certificates include the corresponding number of ECTS credits, providing formal recognition of the training completed through the programme.

This can be useful for doctoral researchers who need evidence of additional academic training as part of their doctoral development.

Financial Support for Participants

The programme provides financial assistance to support participation, although applicants should note that this is not presented as a full doctoral scholarship covering all living and study expenses.

Support for Swiss-Based PhD Candidates

For PhD candidates based in Switzerland, travel expenses are reimbursed based on the cost of a half-fare second-class ticket.

Support for International PhD Candidates

International PhD candidates can receive financial assistance for travel of up to CHF 200 per session, for a maximum of five sessions.

This means eligible international participants could potentially receive up to CHF 1,000 in travel support across five sessions, subject to the programme’s applicable conditions.

Accommodation Support

LIVES also indicates that accommodation subsidies are available for a limited number of students.

International applicants who require accommodation assistance should contact the programme for further information.

Applicants from outside Switzerland are specifically asked in the application form whether they wish to request financial assistance for accommodation.

Meals and Breaks

The programme also provides some meal-related support.

During workshops, lunch breaks are covered.

During the LIVES Doctoriales, lunch and coffee breaks are covered.

Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the programme’s financial arrangements and contact LIVES if they require clarification regarding expenses that are not specifically listed as covered.

Eligibility Requirements

Applicants must satisfy several conditions before applying.

1. Your PhD Must Have a Life Course or Life Span Perspective

The doctoral thesis must incorporate a life course or lifespan perspective.

This is one of the most important eligibility requirements.

Simply being a doctoral student in a social science or health-related field is not enough. The research itself should meaningfully engage with life course or lifespan concepts.

2. Academic Discipline

The doctoral research should have a disciplinary background in an eligible or related field.

The call specifically mentions:

  • Sociology
  • Demography
  • Psychology
  • Epidemiology
  • Economics
  • Political Science
  • Neuroscience
  • History
  • Gender Studies

Related fields may also be considered where the doctoral project has a clear connection to life course research.

3. Existing Academic Affiliation

Applicants must already be affiliated with an academic institution.

This means the programme is intended for people who are already doctoral candidates rather than individuals who are merely planning to start a PhD in the future.

An official document confirming academic affiliation must be submitted with the application.

4. PhD Funding

The PhD thesis must be funded for the length of the doctoral programme.

Funding can come from:

  • An academic institution; or
  • Third-party funding.

Applicants should therefore ensure that their existing doctoral funding arrangement covers the required period.

5. English Language Ability

Applicants must be able to speak and write English fluently.

The minimum stated level is B2.

Because the programme involves workshops, academic presentations, discussions and written research materials, applicants should be comfortable communicating their research in English.

Where Can Applicants Be Based?

The programme is open to doctoral students based in Switzerland and Europe.

The call does not specify a particular racial, ethnic or nationality restriction.

Therefore, eligibility is primarily determined by the applicant’s academic status, institutional affiliation, research topic, funding and geographical location rather than race.

International applicants outside Switzerland can receive certain travel assistance, subject to the programme’s funding conditions.

Why This Programme Could Be Valuable for PhD Researchers

The LIVES Doctoral Programme offers several potential academic and professional advantages.

Interdisciplinary Training

Life course research often crosses disciplinary boundaries. The programme brings together researchers from different academic backgrounds, allowing participants to encounter theories and methods beyond their primary discipline.

Advanced Methodological Skills

The methodological workshops focus on longitudinal and life course analysis, which can strengthen a researcher’s ability to analyse changes and developments over time.

Expert Academic Feedback

Participants have opportunities to present their research to senior scholars and receive specialised feedback.

This can be extremely valuable during the early stages of a PhD, when research questions, theoretical frameworks and methodologies are still being refined.

International Academic Network

The programme creates a community of international PhD researchers working on related questions.

Building relationships with other doctoral researchers can lead to future collaborations, research exchanges, conference opportunities and broader academic networks.

Exposure to Leading Life Course Research

Participants can deepen their understanding of life course theories, concepts and research methods through structured sessions and workshops.

Formal Recognition

Certificates and ECTS credits provide formal recognition of participation in the programme’s training modules.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Applicants should carefully assess whether the programme fits their current doctoral situation.

First, this is not an opportunity for someone who has not yet started a PhD. The applicant must already be affiliated with an academic institution.

Second, the PhD must be funded for the duration of the programme.

Third, the research must genuinely incorporate a life course or lifespan perspective. Applicants should therefore avoid presenting a project that only has a superficial connection to the topic.

Fourth, participation involves in-person attendance in Switzerland. Candidates should consider their ability to attend the required sessions and workshops.

Finally, applicants should not assume that the travel assistance represents complete financial coverage. The call specifies particular limits for travel and indicates that accommodation subsidies are available only to a limited number of students.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

A competitive application should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant’s doctoral research and the objectives of the LIVES programme.

Make the Life Course Connection Explicit

Do not assume that the selection committee will automatically see the connection.

Explain precisely how the thesis examines:

  • Change over time
  • Life transitions
  • Trajectories
  • Turning points
  • Accumulation or depletion
  • Age and ageing
  • Intergenerational processes
  • Longitudinal patterns
  • Policy implications across the life span

Strengthen the Motivation Letter

The cover letter should go beyond saying that the programme is prestigious or interesting.

Explain specifically why LIVES is relevant to the doctoral project and identify the theoretical or methodological skills you hope to develop.

Prepare the Supervisor Early

Because a supervisor support letter is required, applicants should approach their supervisor well before the deadline.

Waiting until the final days could create unnecessary delays.

Make the 500-Word Abstract Count

The abstract has a maximum of approximately 500 words, so every paragraph should have a purpose.

A strong abstract should quickly establish the research problem, research question, theoretical perspective, methodology and expected contribution.

Demonstrate Methodological Interest

Because the programme includes several methodological workshops, applicants should explain how longitudinal or life course methods could strengthen their research.

Conclusion

The LIVES Doctoral Programme 2026–2029 is a valuable academic development opportunity for early-stage PhD researchers whose work examines people’s lives, trajectories and transitions over time.

Through theoretical training, methodological workshops, doctoral presentations, individual expert feedback and an international peer network, the programme offers participants an opportunity to strengthen both the conceptual and practical dimensions of their doctoral research.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to researchers working in sociology, demography, psychology, epidemiology, economics, political science, neuroscience, history, gender studies, health sciences and related disciplines, provided that their doctoral research incorporates a meaningful life course or lifespan perspective.

Applicants should remember that they must already be affiliated with an academic institution, have appropriate funding for their PhD, meet the English-language requirement and be able to participate in the programme’s in-person activities.

Most importantly, prospective applicants should begin preparing their supporting documents early, especially the supervisor recommendation and official academic affiliation document.

Application deadline: 30 September 2026.

For eligible doctoral researchers interested in life course research, longitudinal methods and interdisciplinary academic development, the LIVES Doctoral Programme represents an opportunity to become part of an established international research community while gaining specialised training that can strengthen their PhD journey and future academic career.
